claim: Israel was imposed on the land by outside powers, and the Jews took the land by force in 1948.

heard.who: Rashid Khalidi, historian, in a 2024 interview
heard.quote: pushing through the partition resolution, which is the birth certificate of the state of Israel, the 1947 General Assembly resolution, partitioning Palestine

answer: The idea of splitting Palestine came first from a British commission in 1937; Arab leaders rejected it. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13. The Jewish state would have had about 56 percent of the land, including the Negev desert, when Jews were about a third of the people and held about 6 percent by registered ownership; Arabs held about 48 percent and the rest was public land. The Jewish Agency accepted; Palestinian Arab leaders rejected the plan. Fighting began at once. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and Arab armies entered on 15 May. By 1949 Israel held about 78 percent of the former mandate.

could_not_verify: The text of the Peel report itself: the Avalon page did not load. Peel is cited only through reference works and a UN secretariat paper.
The peace offer in Israel's declaration of independence: Avalon's text has it, but I found no second readable page, so I left it out of the facts.
A third reliable source for the Arab League cable's stated aims beyond the cable itself (the other two cited are a history magazine and an educational site).

Claims that Jewish forces took territory beyond the plan before 15 May appear on a UN Division for Palestinian Rights page, which counts as advocacy; I found no independent readable source and omitted it.
Khalidi's book is not cited (no authorised readable copy); his 2024 interview is used.
Dissent among Arab states beyond Transjordan (for example Egypt's and Syria's reluctance): I did not find a readable source.

The Ad Hoc Committee's sub-committee 2 report (A/AC.14/32, appendix VI) and the Survey of Palestine land tables themselves: not readable. The ownership figures are taken from Imseis's footnote to that report. The UNSCOP population table is read directly (un.org).

How much of the Jewish state was Negev: no scholarly or UN source gives a percentage that I could read. The 'about 60 percent' figure is from the Jewish Virtual Library (advocacy) and the AIJAC page (advocacy). It is attributed, not asserted.

The state-land share of Palestine: Imseis's footnote implies about 47 percent public land (the remainder after Jewish and Arab holdings); I did not compute it on the card. The Jewish Virtual Library's 70 percent refers only to land in what became Israel.

Reliable sources for facts 11 and 12 (Arab League aims, Transjordan): fact 11 has one reliable source (the UN cable itself), the other two are anonymous history sites; fact 12 has two scholarly sources. I found no third readable scholarly page.
Relabelled as 'other' (no named author or institution): History Skills, Explaining History, OnWar, Fanack, War History Online.

Facts still under three reliable sources: the Arab League cable (one reliable, the cable itself), Transjordan (two scholarly), and state land (Imseis's footnote and the mandate text via UNSCOP; the 70 percent figure is advocacy only).
not_claimed: This card does not claim the UN vote made the 1948 war or the later displacement of Palestinians right, wrong or inevitable.
It does not claim the vote was free of great-power pressure or that Palestinian Arabs were consulted in the way they wanted.
It does not claim Jewish forces took only land the plan gave them; Israel ended up with more.
It does not say who fired first in the civil war that followed the vote.

answer_claims.says: The idea of splitting Palestine came first from a British commission in 1937; Arab leaders rejected it.
On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13.

The Jewish state would have had about 56 percent of the land, including the Negev desert, when Jews were about a third of the people and held about 6 percent by registered ownership; Arabs held about 48 percent and the rest was public land.
The Jewish Agency accepted; Palestinian Arab leaders rejected the plan.
Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and Arab armies entered on 15 May.
By 1949 Israel held about 78 percent of the former mandate.

skeptic.notes: Round three (final). Checked: the UNSCOP page, Imseis, Kamel, the cable, and the relabelling. FIXED: the shares are now primary or scholarly. UNSCOP gives the population ('at the end of 1946 ... Jews, 608,000 ... total, 1,846,000', 32.96 percent); Imseis says the plan allotted about 57 percent of the total area of Palestine and that Jews held 5.6 percent by registered ownership on British records of 1945 (percent of the whole land, Arabs 48 percent, the rest public); Kamel gives 56.47 percent of total land. The card says 'of the land' and 'registered ownership', which matches. Negev and state land are on the card. Relabelling explainer sites 'other' is right (no named author). NOT FIXED: (1) fact 11, the Arab League's aims, has one reliable source, the cable itself; the other two are 'other' sites. (2) fact 12 (Abdullah) has two reliable sources, Shlaim and Karsh, who are the two sides of the dispute; the third is an 'other' site. (3) fact 14 (public land) has two: Imseis and a UNSCOP line that only quotes the mandate's text on state lands; the 70 percent figure is Jewish Virtual Library (advocacy). (4) fact 13: the 'about 60 percent desert' share is advocacy only; UNSCOP's quote describes the Negeb's climate, not the plan's share. (5) the card leans on two authors, Imseis and Kamel, both writing from the Palestinian side, for the shares, and has no Israeli-side scholar on them; (6) nit: fact 10's Imseis quote (force numbers) does not match the fact text. Still missing: Jewish forces' gains before 15 May. Stronger attack: pro-Israel (state-land and desert context thinly sourced; 'imposed' is answered only by Saudi and Khalidi, both holders on one side); the pro-Palestinian attack is now largely answered. Contested entries are objects with real quotes from holders.
